parole.significato: A pupil / student in the German education system who is taking, or who has taken and passed, the Abitur.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Abiturient, from Latin abituriō (“to wish to leave”).

parole.significato: A pungent, acrid, poisonous liquid aldehyde, CH₂=CH-CH=O, made by the destructive distillation of glycerol.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Acrolein, from Latin acer (“sharp”) + oleō (“smell”, verb) + -in.

parole.significato: A string stop on an organ with a very soft tone.
parole.testo: From German Aeoline, from Classical Latin Aeolus (see Aeolian harp) + German -ine. Piecewise doublet of aeolina.

parole.significato: Any of several cherries cultivated from the sour cherry, distinguished from morellos by colorless juice.
parole.testo: From German Amarelle, from Medieval Latin amārellum, from Latin amārus (“bitter, sour”) + -ellum (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: The coexistence of opposing attitudes or feelings (such as love and hate) towards a person, object or idea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Ambivalenz (“simultaneous conflicting feelings”), from Latin ambi- (“both”) and valentia (“strength”), from the verb valere (“to be strong”) (see valiant); spelled on the model of French-origin words ending in -ence. The German term was coined by Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler

parole.significato: Simultaneously experiencing or expressing opposing or contradictory feelings, beliefs, motivations, or meanings.
parole.testo: Back-formation from ambivalence, from German Ambivalenz, from Latin ambi- (“in two ways”) + valeō (“be strong”); equivalent to ambi- + -valent. Compare ambivert.

parole.significato: The intentional feature by which something indirectly given to consciousness is experienced as co-present or implied al…
parole.testo: From German Appräsentation, coined by Edmund Husserl from appräsentieren, from Latin ad- + praesentatio.

parole.significato: Stating that which is actual, usually in contrast with modal sentences.
parole.testo: Calque of German assertorisch (“assertory”) (itself a calque of Latin assertōrius using using Latin assert- (supine stem of asserō) + -orisch (“-ory”), popularized by Immanuel Kant). By surface analysis, assertor + -ic. See German -orisch.

parole.significato: Knowledge of the stars, especially the fixed stars; the branch of astronomy dealing with the fixed stars.
parole.testo: From astro- (prefix meaning ‘star’) + -gnosy (suffix denoting the scientific knowledge of a subject), modelled on German Astrognosie, or its etymon Late Latin astrognosia, from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “celestial body; (specifically) fixed star; planet”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to barbituric acid or its derivatives.
parole.testo: From German Barbiturat. Perhaps from the name Barbara, or perhaps from Latin. The second element is uric.

parole.significato: A flowering plant of species Anacyclus pyrethrum.
parole.testo: From German Bertram (according to Kluge appearing first in English in 1578), well-known, from Middle High German bërtram, bërhtram, from Old High German bërhtram, from Latin pyrethrum, from Ancient Greek πύρεθρον (púrethron).

parole.significato: An extremely potent nerve toxin produced by the anaerobic bacteria Clostridium botulinum. Ingesting botulin results in…
parole.testo: From German Botulin, from Latin botulus (“sausage”).

parole.significato: Poisoning caused by the toxin from Clostridium botulinum, an anaerobic bacterium that grows in improperly prepared food.
parole.testo: From German Botulismus, from Latin botulus (“sausage”), the first identified source of the disease, + -ism.

parole.significato: The theories and practices of the cameralists.
parole.testo: From German Kameralismus, from Medieval Latin cameralis + Latin -ismus (“-ism”). First element is from camera (“chamber”) (English camera), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára).

parole.significato: A public administrative servant of continental rulers of the 17th and 18th centuries who was a mercantilist and advocat…
parole.testo: From German Kameralist, from New Latin cameralista, from Medieval Latin cameralis + Latin -ista (“-ist”), from camera (“chamber”) (English camera), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára). Sense is due to administrators in the royal chamber; compare political sense of cabinet.

parole.significato: A chemical compound found in chilli peppers, which is responsible for their piquancy.
parole.testo: Arbitrary alteration of earlier capsicine, capsicin (“material extracted from cayenne pepper”), presumably to prevent confusion, from German Capsicin, from New Latin capsicum + German -in. Name introduced by John Clough Thresh (1850–1932) in “Capsaicin, the Active Principle of Capsicum Fruits”.

parole.significato: A volatile alkaloid extracted from Capsicum annuum or from capsaicin.
parole.testo: From German Capsicin, from New Latin Capsicum + German -in.

parole.significato: A betaine, 3-hydroxy-4-trimethylammonio-butanoate, that is found in the liver and has a function in fatty acid transpor…
parole.testo: From German Carnitin, coined from Latin carn- + Latin -i- + -t- (“arbitrary insertion”) + -in, for it was first described in meat extracts in 1905. By surface analysis, Latin carnit- + -ine.

parole.significato: The overseer of a hundred (zent) in medieval France and Germany.
parole.testo: From German Zentgraf, from Latin cent- (“100”) + German -graf (“-grave”).

parole.significato: Stimulating the production of bile by the liver.
parole.testo: From German cholereticum, from modern Latin choleresis (“bile secretion from the liver”) (modelled on diuretic).

parole.significato: A monogram that forms an abbreviation for the name of Jesus Christ, traditionally used as a Christian symbol, such as t…
parole.testo: From Christo- + gram, c. 1900, adopted from German Christogramm, in c. 1860 as portmanteau or abbreviation of the slightly older (1840s) and more formal compound Christusmonogramm, translating the Medieval Latin monogramma Christi. English literature before 1900 used compositional "Monogram of Chris

parole.significato: A keyboard, especially of a musical instrument.
parole.testo: From German Klaviatur, ultimately from Latin clāvis (“key”).

parole.significato: An early keyboard instrument producing a soft sound by means of metal blades (called tangents) attached to the inner en…
parole.testo: From German Klavichord, from Renaissance Latin clavichordium, from clāvis (“key”) + chorda (“cord, string”).

parole.significato: An elite group of intellectuals; learned people, the literati.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek κλῆρος (klêros) + -isy. Introduced by Coleridge, based on German Clerisei (modern Klerisei), from Late Latin clēricus.

parole.significato: Pertaining to an utterance relaying information and likely to be regarded as true or false.
parole.testo: Coined to translate the German konstatierend, using cōnstāt-, the perfect passive participial stem of the Latin verb cōnstō (“to agree, correspond, or fit; to am certain, decided, or consistent”), suffixed with the English -ive, suggesting a hypothetical Latin etymon of the form *cōnstātīvus.

parole.significato: An igneous, volcanic rock with a high iron content.
parole.testo: From German Dazit, from Latin Dācia (“greater Romania”). First used in 1863 by Austrian geologists Franz von Hauer and Guido Stache, in a description of the geology of Transylvania.

parole.significato: schizophrenia
parole.testo: A Latin term coined by Arnold Pick in 1891, first used in German and later adopted into English. From the Latin dēmentia (“madness; insanity”) + praecox (“premature; untimely”, whence English precocious), together meaning “untimely madness” or “premature dementia”. Here, dēmentia carries the connota

parole.significato: An organism that feeds on detritus.
parole.testo: From German Detritivore, from Latin dētrītus (“the act of rubbing away”) (from dēterō (“to rub away, to rub off, to wear out”), from dē- (“away; down”) + terō (“to rub; to wear away, to wear out”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, to rub by twisting; to twist, to turn”)) + Latin vorāre (fr

parole.significato: A dogmatic decree or command, especially issued by one who rules without popular consent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Diktat, from Latin dictātum (“that which has been dictated”), from the perfect passive participle of dictō (“dictate”). Doublet of dictate. Originally used with reference to Germany's penalties as dictated by the Treaty of Versailles.

parole.significato: Major; in the major mode.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Dur.

parole.significato: The outer layer of a pollen grain or spore; the exosporium.
parole.testo: From German Exine, from Latin ex- + German -ine.

parole.significato: A geologic structure formed by erosion or normal faulting on a thrust system; a tectonic window.
parole.testo: From German Fenster (“window”), from Latin fenestra (“window”).

parole.significato: A gathering for a specified reason or occasion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Fest (“feast, festival, party”), from Middle High German fëst, from Latin festum, from which last are also English feast, festival, festivity, fete, fiesta (see these).

parole.significato: A warm dry wind blowing down the north sides of the Alps, especially in Switzerland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Föhn, from Old High German phonno, from Vulgar Latin faōnius, an alteration of Latin favōnius (“west wind”), from Favōnius (“Roman wind god”).

parole.significato: An introductory section preceding the main text of a book or other document; especially, one written by another person…
parole.testo: Morphologically fore- + word. Calque of German Vorwort, itself a calque of Latin praefatio (“preface”). Cognate with German Low German Vörwoord (“foreword”), Dutch voorwoord (“foreword”), West Frisian foarwurd (“foreword”), Danish forord (“preface; proviso”), Swedish förord (“foreword”). Compare als

parole.significato: Synonym of formative (“language unit, typically a morph, that has a morphological function”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Formans, from Latin elementum fōrmāns (“forming element”), with fōrmāns being the present participle of fōrmō (“to shape; to form; to fashion”). Doublet of formant.

parole.significato: A band of frequencies in a sound spectrum that have greater intensity and determine the quality of a sound, especially…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Formant, from Latin fōrmāns (“shaping; forming; fashioning”), present participle of fōrmō (“to shape; to form; to fashion”). Doublet of formans.

parole.significato: A style of black letter type, used especially in German-speaking countries from the 16th century until World War II.
parole.testo: First appears c. 1886 as fractur, and c. 1904 as fraktur, from German Fraktur, from Latin frāctūra (“breaking”, noun), from frangere (“to break”), past participle fractus. Compare English fracture, fraction. Doublet of fracture.

parole.significato: A self-ruling city within the Holy Roman Empire that had some autonomy and was represented in the Imperial Diet.
parole.testo: A calque of German Freie Reichsstadt (short singular form of Freie und Reichsstädte) or Latin urbs imperialis libera.

parole.significato: Any of several obsolete European silver coins.
parole.testo: From German Groschen, from Middle High German grosse, from Medieval Latin (denarius) grossus (“thick (penny)”).

parole.significato: The study of heuristic methods and principles.
parole.testo: From heuristic, from German heuristisch, from New Latin heuristicus by irregular formation from Ancient Greek εὑρίσκω (heurískō, “I discover”).

parole.significato: The now-discredited principle that the body will not harm itself by its own immune reactions.
parole.testo: Latinate neologism coined c. 1900 by Paul Ehrlich in German, from Latin horror, auto- (“self”), toxicus (“toxic”). Compare horror vacui.

parole.significato: A dictionary of a specific dialect, or of the words and phrases peculiar to one part of a country.
parole.testo: PIE word  *swé Borrowed from German Idiotikon, Idioticon (archaic), from Late Latin idioticon (chiefly in the titles of works), from Ancient Greek ἰδιωτικόν (idiōtikón), the neuter singular of ἰδιωτικός (idiōtikós, “pertaining to or for a person not engaged in public affairs; private; amateurish”),

parole.significato: The withdrawal of a person within a routine that they cannot escape, a forerunner of pathological melancholia.
parole.testo: From German Inkludenz, a 1960s neologism coined by Hubertus Tellenbach, derived from Latin inclūdō (“confine, imprison”).

parole.significato: A set of instruments, a toolset.
parole.testo: From instrument + -arium, originally after German Instrumentarium, itself after New Latin īnstrūmentārium.

parole.significato: Self-referentiality.
parole.testo: From German Ipsissimosität, coined in 1886 by Friedrich Nietzsche from the Latin ipsissima (“very own”).

parole.significato: Yeast which tends to form on fermented foods, such as sauerkraut.
parole.testo: From German Kahm, from Middle High German kan, from Vulgar Latin cana, from Latin cānus (“gray”).

parole.significato: A United States Military barracks or installation in Germany.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Kaserne (“barracks”), ultimately from Latin quaterna through French caserne.

parole.significato: A type of crescent-shaped biscuit or bread roll.
parole.testo: From German Kipfel, diminutive of Kipf (“wagon post”), from Old High German kipfa, chipf, from Latin cippus (“post”).

parole.significato: German culture or civilization, especially seen as authoritarian or racist during the period of world wars (1914-18 and…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Kultur, from Latin cultūra; doublet of culture.

parole.significato: An avalanche.
parole.testo: Borrowed by Lord Byron from German Lawine, from Late Latin lābīna, from Latin lābēs (“fall”).

parole.significato: A broad volcanic crater, usually filled with water to form a lake.
parole.testo: English usage from 1825, from German Maar, of uncertain origin (see the German entry for theories), possibly from Vulgar Latin *mara (“standing water”), from Latin mare (“sea”), and thus a Doublet of mare (“a large, dark plain; a lake on Titan”) and mere (“a body of standing water”).

parole.significato: A person of great skill or authority in a particular field.
parole.testo: From German Meister (“master, highly skilled tradesman; champion”), from Old High German meistar, from Latin magister, whence also English master, mister, magister, and maestro, making all these words doublets of each other.

parole.significato: In the International System of Units, the base unit of amount of substance; the amount of substance of a system which c…
parole.testo: Calqued from German Mol; spelled as if it had come directly from molecule or Latin moles (the ultimate source of Mol and molecule in any event).

parole.significato: minor; in the minor key.
parole.testo: From German Moll, from Latin mollis (“soft, tender, elegiac”). Compare molle (“flat (in music)”). Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål moll.

parole.significato: A hallucinogenic alkaloid present in the fly agaric and other related fungi; 3-hydroxy-5-aminomethylisoxazole.
parole.testo: From German Muscimol, from Latin musc(arius) (in Amanita muscaria) + im(ine) + -ol.

parole.significato: A silvery elemental metal with an atomic number of 28 and symbol Ni.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Nickel, first used in a text by the Swedish mineralogist Axel F. Cronstedt as an abbreviation of Kupfernickel (“a mineral containing copper and nickel”), from Kupfer (“copper”) + Nickel (“insignificant person, goblin”), originally nickname of Nikolaus (“Nicholas”), due to the de

parole.significato: A solution of sulfur trioxide in sulfuric acid.
parole.testo: From German Oleum, from Latin oleum (“olive oil”), from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”). Doublet of oil.

parole.significato: A proponent of the theories and ideals of ordoliberalism (“a political philosophy that emphasizes the desirability of t…
parole.testo: Probably a back-formation from ordoliberalism, borrowed from German Ordoliberalismus (coined in 1950 by the German economist Hero Moeller (1892–1974)), from ORDO (the name of a journal, the full title of which is ORDO — Jahrbuch für die Ordnung von Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft (ORDO – Yearbook of Eco

parole.significato: A political philosophy that emphasizes the desirability of the government establishing rules to maximize the potential…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Ordoliberalismus (coined in 1950 by the German economist Hero Moeller (1892–1974)), from ORDO (the name of a journal, the full title of which is ORDO — Jahrbuch für die Ordnung von Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft (ORDO – Yearbook of Economic and Social Order) + Liberalismus (“libera

parole.significato: The belief that all matter is conscious in some form.
parole.testo: From pan- + psychism, a calque of German Panpsychismus (1874), from New Latin pampsychia coined by Francisco Patrizi in his 1591 Nova de Universis Philosophia, from Ancient Greek πᾰν- (păn-, “all”) + ψυχή (psukhḗ, “mind, life force, soul”) + -ία (-ía, “-ia: forming abstract nouns”). Cognate with Anc

parole.significato: A freshman at a German university.
parole.testo: From German Pennal, from Latin penna (“feather, quill”).

parole.significato: A substance similar to marzipan, but produced from peach or apricot pits instead of almonds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Persipan, a blend of Latin persicus (“peach (tree)”) and German Marzipan.

parole.significato: The study of orders, fraternity, and award items.
parole.testo: From German Phaleristik, from Latin phalera, from Ancient Greek Φάληρος (Phálēros, “Phalerus, a mythological hero”).

parole.significato: A person who is ignorant or uneducated; specifically, a person who lacks appreciation of or is antagonistic towards art…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Philistine, influenced by philister, Philister (“(historical) in German universities: person not associated with the university; person who lacks appreciation of or is antagonistic towards art or culture”), from German Philister (“person from ancient Philistia; (figurative,

parole.significato: A mass of cytoplasm, containing many nuclei, created by the aggregation of amoeboid cells of slime molds during their v…
parole.testo: From German Plasmodium, from Latin plasma.

parole.significato: A college course designed to give a student supervised practical knowledge of a subject previously studied theoreticall…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Praktikum, a coinage from the neuter of Late Latin practicus (“practical”), from Ancient Greek πρακτικός (praktikós, “of or pertaining to action, concerned with action or business, active, practical”), from πράσσω (prássō, “to do”).

parole.significato: The act of making something present to consciousness that is not originally given; a synonym of presentification; an in…
parole.testo: From German Präsentation, from Latin praesentatio. In the phenomenological sense, a calque of German Vergegenwärtigung.

parole.significato: A toasted bread or cracker usually in the shape of a loose knot.
parole.testo: From dialectal German Pretzel, a variant of standard Brezel, from Old High German brēzitella, from Vulgar Latin *brāchiātellus, diminutive of Latin brāchium, bracchium (“arm”); named for the appearance of folded arms.

parole.significato: The transfer of a company or organization from government to private ownership and control.
parole.testo: Calque of German Privatisierung (with English -ation), derived from Latin prīvātus (“apart from the state; private”), with reference to post-First World War German economic principles. Popularized by Sidney Merlin in 1943, who was aware of the term reprivatization (used in similar contexts), already

parole.significato: A red pigment produced by certain bacteria.
parole.testo: From German Prodigiosin, from Latin prodigiosus + -in.

parole.significato: One who administers the Eucharist with leavened bread, in particular a member of the Eastern Orthodox Church.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Prozymit, from Medieval Latin prozymīta, from Byzantine Greek προζυμίτης (prozumítēs), from Ancient Greek προζύμιον (prozúmion, “leaven”) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs, suffix forming masculine nouns meaning being connected to or a member of something, or coming from a particular place). προ

parole.significato: A preliminary treaty or contract.
parole.testo: From German Punktation, from Medieval Latin punctatio.

parole.significato: A scanning pattern of parallel lines that form the display of an image projected on a cathode-ray tube of a television…
parole.testo: From German Raster, from Latin rāster, from rāstrum (“rake”, noun), from rādō (“to scrape”, verb).

parole.significato: The consideration of an abstract thing as if it were concrete, or of an inanimate object as if it were living.
parole.testo: First attested around 1846; a macaronic calque of German Verdinglichung, using -ification (“making”) for ver- + -lich + -ung, and Latin rēs (“thing”) for Ding (“thing”)

parole.significato: To regard something abstract as if it were a concrete material thing.
parole.testo: Back-formation from reification, calque from German. Formed as Latin rēs (“thing”) + -ify (English suffix).

parole.significato: A pipe organ stop of 4-foot or 2-foot pitch.
parole.testo: From German, from Latin salix (“willow”) + French -et.

parole.significato: A labial pipe organ stop of eight-foot pitch.
parole.testo: From German Salizional, from Latin salix (“willow”) + -al.

parole.significato: ammonium chloride
parole.testo: From German Salmiak, from Latin sal ammoniacum. Doublet of sal ammoniac.

parole.significato: Half of a school year (US) or academic year such as autumn or spring semester.
parole.testo: From German Semester, from New Latin sēmestris (“lasting six months”), from sex (“six”) + mēnsis (“month”).

parole.significato: A class held for advanced studies in which students meet regularly to discuss original research, under the guidance of…
parole.testo: From German Seminar, from Latin sēminārium, from sēmen (“seed”). Compare seminary.

parole.significato: A sensory receptor in certain invertebrates, especially arthropods.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Sensillum, from New Latin sensillum, diminutive of Latin sēnsus (“perception, feeling”). Coined by German zoologist Ernst Haeckel in Systematische Phylogenie (1895).

parole.significato: The Chinese people or a Chinese person, (particularly) with reference to the historical southern Chinese known to the G…
parole.testo: From German Sinese (“a Chinese person”), from Sina (“China”) + -ese (“-ese: forming demonyms”), from Medieval Latin Sina (“China”) + -ensis (“-ese: forming adjs”), from Latin Sinae (“the Southern Chinese, Southern China”), from Ancient Greek. Equivalent to Sino- + -ese.

parole.significato: Any powder (originally containing gypsum plaster and glue) that when mixed with water forms a plastic paste, which is u…
parole.testo: From Spackle, originally a brand name, perhaps based on German Spachtel which is ultimately from Latin spatula. Doublet of spatula.

parole.significato: A discipline, principally within applied mathematics, concerned with the systematic study of the collection, presentati…
parole.testo: From German Statistik, from New Latin statisticum (“of the state”) and Italian statista (“statesman, politician”), compare English statist. Statistik introduced by Gottfried Achenwall (1749), originally designated the analysis of data about the state.

parole.significato: Of a habitat: of an altitude, latitude, or type just below that which would be permanently covered by snow (the snow li…
parole.testo: PIE word  *upó From sub- (prefix meaning ‘beneath, under’) + nival (“abounding with snow; snow-covered, snowy; found or thriving in snowy conditions”), borrowed from German subnival, from Late Latin subnivalis, from Latin sub- (prefix meaning ‘beneath, under’) + nivālis (“snow-covered; snowy”) (from

parole.significato: The supplying of something lacking.
parole.testo: From German Suppletivwesen, from Latin supplēre (“to supply”), perfect stem supplet-, + -ion.

parole.significato: The science or study of systematizing
parole.testo: From German Systematologie, from Late Latin systemat-, stem of systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma, “organised whole, body”); with suffix -logie (“study of”).

parole.significato: Any of a very large class of naturally occurring and synthetic organic compounds formally derived from the hydrocarbon…
parole.testo: From German Terpen, coined by August Kekulé in 1866 in analogy to German Terpentin, from Latin terebinthina. Piecewise doublet of terpin; compare also terebinth and turpentine.

parole.significato: A one-thirtieth tax introduced in the Duchy of Württemberg in 1691.
parole.testo: From the German Tricesimation, ultimately from the Latin trīcēsimus (“thirtieth”).

parole.significato: A female water-sprite or nymph.
parole.testo: From German Undine, from New Latin undīna, from Latin unda (“wave”).

parole.significato: A homosexual person, especially a man.
parole.testo: From German Urning, from Latin Uranus; see Uranian for more.

parole.significato: Free to move about.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German vagil, from Latin vagus (“wandering”).

parole.significato: The combining capacity of an atom, functional group, or radical determined by the number of atoms of hydrogen with whic…
parole.testo: Etymology 1, noun sense 1.1 (“combining capacity of an atom”) and etymology 1, noun sense 3 (“one-dimensional value assigned by a person to an object, situation, or state”) are borrowed from German Valenz + English -ence (suffix meaning ‘having the condition or state of’). Valenz is a clipping of Qu

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or as a result of vicariance
parole.testo: From German vikarierend, present participle of vikarieren (“to act as a substitute”), from Vikar (“vicar, representative”), ultimately from Latin vicārius (“substitute”).

parole.significato: A musical instrument consisting of a flat sounding box with numerous strings placed on a horizontal surface, played wit…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Zither, from Old High German zithara, from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára, “a kind of harp”). Doublet of cithara, cither, and guitar.
